background.definition: Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acute, often symmetric, usually ascending and paralyzing illness caused by autoimmune inflammation of peripheral nerves.

list.listitem: Worldwide occurrence, with an incidence of 0.6 to 4.0/100,000 per year. More males affected than females (ratio 1.5-2.0:1).
Slight peak in late adolescence and again in the elderly.
Known to occur in all ages although rare in infancy.
GBS is the most common cause of acute neuromuscular paralysis.

Autonomic dysfunction, including tachycardia (most common), urinary retention, hypertension alternating with hypotension, orthostatic hypotension, bradycardia, and other arrhythmias occur in approximately 70%.

About 70% of patients report an antecedent acute infectious illness, most commonly a respiratory tract infection or gastroenteritis that has resolved by the time symptoms begin. Campylobacter jejuni infection is the most commonly identified antecedent infection.
There is also an association with infection by Haemophilus influenzae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and cytomegalovirus (CMV).
In the Netherlands, 5% of patients with GBS have an associated acute Hepatitis E viral infection.

Influenza vaccination is associated with a small but significantly increased risk of hospitalization because of GBS, estimated at 1.6 excess cases of GBS for every 1,000,000 people vaccinated with H1N1.

GBS has been reported following vaccination for SARS-CoV-2. It appears to be more common following vaccination with the Ad26.COV.2 (Johnson and Johnson) vaccine (3.3 cases/million doses) than with mRNA vaccines (0.3 cases/million doses).
The pathophysiology is essentially unknown.
The proposed mechanism is that an antecedent infection evokes an immune response, which in turn cross-reacts with peripheral nerves (molecular mimicry).
The immune response can be directed toward the myelin or the axon of peripheral nerves.
Multifocal inflammatory demyelination occurs, starting at the level of the nerve roots, seen earliest at the nodes of Ranvier.
Cellular and humoral immune responses participate.
Activated T-cell invasion is followed by macrophage-mediated demyelination.

Patients whose GBS occurred within 42 days of influenza or toxoid containing vaccine should only receive these vaccines in the future if benefit clearly outweighs potential harm. However, many patients with a history of GBS not following vaccination also (inappropriately) decline future vaccinations. C
While there is a possible but very small increase in risk of GBS following messenger RNA vaccine for COVID, the benefits of the vaccine far outweight any potential harms.B

Elevated CSF protein and normal WBC are typical, as are abnormalities in nerve conduction studies. C

Differential.Differential_Features: May cause fixed and dilated pupils (50%) and prominent cranial nerve dysfunction
Usually occurs in epidemics; fever and meningismus common
Ascending paralysis but sparing of sensation
Headache, fever, and asymmetric flaccid paralysis but sparing of sensation
Prolonged back pain and sphincter disturbances
Sepsis, multiple-organ failure, or long-term ventilation

list.listitem: Rapidly evolving areflexic motor paralysis is seen, with or without a sensory disturbance.
The pattern is usually ascending, first noticed as a gait disturbance.
Weakness evolves over hours to days accompanied by tingling dysesthesias in the extremities.

Bladder dysfunction may occur in severe cases but is usually transient; if bladder dysfunction is a prominent feature and occurs early in the course, other etiologies, particularly spinal cord disease, should be considered.
Elevated protein and normal WBC in CSF (albuminocytologic dissociation) is characteristic, although protein is often normal in first week of illness.

In a case series of 494 adults patients with GBS, the CSF demonstrated a mild pleocytosis (5-50 cells/μL) 15% of the time. However, none of the patients had more than 50 cells/μL. An increased CSF protein concentration was found in only 64% of patients, and became more common with increasing time from the onset of weakness (49% at the first day to 88% after 2 weeks).
Nerve conduction studies initially may show prolonged F-wave latency; conduction block is common in GBS and is characteristic of acquired demyelinating neuropathy.
Two sets of nerve conduction studies (one in the first 2 weeks and the other between weeks 3 and 8 of onset of disease), is sufficient for the electrodiagnosis of GBS.
Perform MRI of the spinal cord if myelopathy or cord lesion are present.
Forced vital capacity: if less than 15 mL/kg, endotracheal intubation is indicated.
Perform CXR for diaphragm weakness.

Six predictors of mechanical ventilation in GBS are: time from onset to admission less than 7 days (OR 2.5), inability to cough (OR 9.1), inability to stand (OR 2.5), inability to lift the elbows (OR 3.0) or head (OR 4.3), and increases in liver enzyme levels (OR 2.1).

The Erasmus Guillain-Barre Syndrome Respiratory insufficiency risk score includes days from onset of weakness to hospital admission (shorter is worse), presence of facial or bulbar weakness at hospital admission, and Medical Research Council sum score at hospital admission (lower is worse) to predict the need for ventilation. It has been prospectively validated. Scores range from 0 to 7 points with respiratory failure in 1% to 90%.
Mechanical ventilation was required in more than 85% of patients with at least four predictors.
Clinical diagnosis is made by recognizing the pattern of rapidly evolving paralysis with areflexia, the absence of constitutional symptoms, and characteristic antecedent events.
If the diagnosis is strongly suspected, treatment should be initiated empirically.
The need for mechanical ventilation is increased with more rapid progression; inability to cough, stand, lift elbows, or head; and elevated liver enzymes.
GBS is a medical emergency requiring constant monitoring and support of vital functions, typically in an intensive care unit. C
If the diagnosis is strongly suspected, treatment should be initiated without waiting for the evolution of characteristic findings to occur. C
Either high-dose IVIg or plasma exchange can be initiated, as they are equally effective; IVIg is slightly safer and much easier to administer.B
Corticosteroids neither hasten recovery nor affect the long-term outcome. B
Plasma exchange is more beneficial when started within 7 days of onset but is still beneficial in patients treated up to 30 days after disease onset. B
The decision as to which immunotherapy to choose (i.e., IVIg vs. plasma exchange) is usually made on the basis of cost, availability, and side effects. IVIg is generally better tolerated.

Either high-dose IVIg or plasma exchange can be initiated, as they are equally effective; a combination of the two is not significantly better than either alone. A systematic review found that IVIg was significantly more likely than placebo to result in symptomatic improvement (OR 2.8, 95% CI 1.4-5.6).
IVIg is usually administered as five daily infusions for a total dose of 2 g/kg body weight; often used as initial therapy secondary to ease of administration.
Plasma exchange of 50 mL/kg body weight is given on a schedule of alternating days.

In mild GBS, two sessions of plasma exchange are significantly superior to none. In moderate GBS, four sessions of plasma exchange are significantly superior to two. In severe GBS, six sessions of plasma exchange are not superior to four. B
Plasma exchange removes any previously administered IVIg, negating its benefits if performed as second line.
IV methylprednisolone alone does not produce significant benefit or harm with GBS, and oral steroids may slow recovery.
Subcutaneous unfractionated or fractionated heparin and support stockings are recommended for nonambulatory adult patients until they become able to walk independently.
Simple analgesics or NSAIDs often do not provide adequate pain relief.
Gabapentin is effective in neuropathic pain and likely ineffective in acute pain.

A recent Cochrane review concluded that evidence for the effectiveness of other immunomodulatory therapies (the use of azathioprine, methotrexate, and interferon-beta) in the treatment of GBS is insufficient to rule out a small or moderate benefit.
A Chinese herbal medicine, tripterygium polyglycoside, compared to glucocorticoids was assocaited with a 47% improvement in revocer after 8 weeks; these results require conformation.
Tracheostomy may be postponed for 2 weeks.
If after 2 weeks the pulmonary function tests do not show any significant improvement from baseline, tracheostomy should be performed.
It is unknown whether azathioprine, interferon-beta, or any other immunosuppressives or treatments are beneficial for acute GBS or chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculopathy.
Treatment in the acute phase should include an individual program of gentle strengthening involving isometric, isotonic, isokinetic, and manual resistive and progressive resistive exercises.
Multidisciplinary rehabilitation has some evidence of benefit in observational studies.
Rehabilitation should be focused on proper limb positioning, posture, orthotics, and nutrition.
An exercise program may be beneficial for persistent fatigue.
Cardiac monitoring for arrhythmias
Respiratory monitoring for possible intubation
Approximately 85% of patients achieve a full functional recovery within several months to a year. B
Minor findings on examination, such as areflexia, may persist. C
The mortality rate is approximately 5%, mostly resulting from pulmonary complications. C
Between 5% and 10% of patients have one or more relapses; such cases are then classified as chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy. C
Immunizations are not recommended during the acute phase of GBS and should probably not be given within 1 year after the onset of disease.
After 1 year, the need for immunization should be reviewed on an individual basis.
If GBS occurs within 6 weeks after a particular immunization, consideration should be given to avoiding that immunization in that individual in the future.
Daily reassurance should be given as to the generally good outlook for recovery.

Mortality among 527 patients with GBS was 2.8% after 6 months and 3.9% after 12 months. Risk factors for death included increasing age, increasing severity of muscle weakness, and the need for mechanical ventilation.
A second peak in incidence in the elderly has been postulated as a failing of immune-suppressor mechanisms.
The prognosis is worse in the elderly.
In younger children, pain is frequently the only symptom they are able to articulate, and evidence of subtle weakness and loss of relexes may be overlooked.
Gait disorder is the most common presentation in children.
A peak in late adolescence and young adulthood coincides with an increased risk of infections with CMV and Campylobacter jejuni.
Disease tends to be milder.
The value of plasma exchange in children younger than 12 years is unknown.
